Q123481708.summary: Against an openwork ground of small crosses, Christ, haloed and bending slightly forward, points to a small child standing at the centre, presenting him to the apostles, among whom Peter can be recognised by his keys. The scene illustrates Christ's teaching that whoever becomes humble like a little child is greatest in the kingdom of heaven, a subject rarely depicted in medieval art. The plaque belongs to the celebrated Magdeburg ivories, made for Emperor Otto I's church in Magdeburg.
facts: It is one of sixteen surviving 'Magdeburg ivories', probably given by Otto I to the church of Saint Maurice at Magdeburg around 968, when it was raised to an archbishopric.

The Louvre notes that the plaque was later remounted on a casket in the Halle treasury (c. 1520–1526) and passed through the collections of Victor Martin Le Roy and Jean-Joseph Marquet de Vasselot before its acquisition in 1993.
The original setting of the series is unknown; an ambo, altar frontal and doors have all been proposed.
Q123481708.notes: Inv. OA 11372. Wikipedia lists this plaque as 'Jesus blesses a little child'; the Louvre identifies the subject as Matthew 18:1–6.
Q123481708.original_title: Plaque ajourée : Le Christ désignant un enfant

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-apsidal-ar.summary: On the arch framing the apse, the Lamb lies on a throne in a medallion at the summit, between the seven candlesticks and the symbols of the evangelists, while below the twenty-four elders in white raise their crowns towards him. The arch translates the throne vision of the Apocalypse directly into mosaic above the altar.
facts: Wikipedia describes the apsidal arch as showing twelve men on each side holding wreaths, with the symbols of the four evangelists surrounding a lamb on a throne, a symbol of Christ's return.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.
